evidence.quote: Length 20 Miles | 32 KM Drive Time 1 Hour

evidence.claim: It is a Washington state scenic byway
evidence.quote: SR 11 is designated as the Chuckanut Drive Scenic Byway, a state scenic byway

evidence.claim: Between Burlington and Bow-Edison, the approach runs past a patchwork of fields. Bow and Edison sit off the drive at Bow Junction, before the coastal section.
evidence.quote: From Burlington to Bow-Edison, this scenic stretch of farmland is home to a patchwork of fields.

evidence.claim: Bow and Edison sit off the drive at Bow Junction
evidence.quote: These small neighboring communities are located off Chuckanut Drive at the Bow Junction.

evidence.claim: The route began as an 1890s logging road connecting the Skagit Valley with Bellingham.
evidence.quote: Originally built as a logging road in the 1890s to connect the Skagit Valley to the growing community of Bellingham

evidence.claim: It opened as a gravel section of the Pacific Highway in spring 1916 and was paved in 1921.
evidence.quote: Chuckanut Drive, a 20-mile-long (32 km) section of the Pacific Highway in the Chuckanut Mountains, was opened as a gravel road during the spring of 1916 and paved in 1921.

evidence.claim: The Pacific Highway became US 99 in 1926.
evidence.quote: When the U.S. route system was formed in 1926, the Pacific Highway became US 99.

evidence.claim: When the main highway shifted inland via Lake Samish in 1931, Chuckanut Drive became US 99 Alternate.
evidence.quote: After an inland bypass was designated by the state to become US 99 in 1931, Chuckanut Drive became U.S. Route 99 Alternate.

evidence.claim: From I-5 north of Burlington, SR 11 travels northwest to Bow and Edison at the head of Samish Bay.
evidence.quote: SR 11 then turns north at a junction with Bow Hill Road (formerly SR 537) near the communities of Edison and Bow at the head of Samish Bay.

evidence.claim: From I-5 north of Burlington, SR 11 travels northwest
evidence.quote: SR 11, also named Chuckanut Drive, begins north of Burlington at a partial cloverleaf interchange with I-5.

evidence.claim: It follows the bay around Blanchard Mountain, passes through Larrabee State Park, then follows Chuckanut Bay.
evidence.quote: turns northwest to follow Samish Bay around the west side of Blanchard Mountain

evidence.claim: passes through Larrabee State Park, then follows Chuckanut Bay
evidence.quote: SR 11 crosses into Whatcom County and travels northwest through Larrabee State Park, the oldest state park in Washington, serving its trailhead parking lots, campgrounds, and a boat launch. Leaving the state park, the highway follows the Interurban Trail along Chuckanut Bay

evidence.claim: The drive descends into Fairhaven on Bellingham Bay before SR 11 turns east to rejoin I-5.
evidence.quote: It travels through a residential neighborhood and descends into Fairhaven, a historic business district on Bellingham Bay

evidence.claim: before SR 11 turns east to rejoin I-5
evidence.quote: The highway turns east onto Old Fairhaven Parkway and travels through a residential neighborhood as it heads uphill along Padden Creek. SR 11 then terminates at an interchange with I-5 in southern Bellingham

evidence.claim: Edison once served as headquarters for a project with a national audience: Equality Colony.
evidence.quote: In 1897, Edison became the headquarters of a national utopian socialist project known as Equality Colony

evidence.claim: The Brotherhood of the Cooperative Commonwealth backed the socialist settlement in 1897.
evidence.quote: In 1897, Edison became the headquarters of a national utopian socialist project known as Equality Colony, backed by an organization known as the Brotherhood of the Cooperative Commonwealth.

evidence.claim: On 280 acres outside town, members farmed and milled timber, with a school and shops for blacksmithing and copper work.
evidence.quote: The socialist colony was established on 280 acres just outside Edison and it engaged in farming and timber milling and included a school as well as blacksmith and copper-working shops.

evidence.claim: Their newspaper, Industrial Freedom, circulated nationally.
evidence.quote: The Edison-based Brotherhood also published a newspaper called Industrial Freedom for national circulation

evidence.claim: The community folded shortly after 1903.
evidence.quote: The socialist community folded shortly after 1903

evidence.claim: Edison now has a concentration of artists and galleries.
evidence.quote: Edison is known for its concentration of artists and galleries

evidence.quote: it was later named for famous inventor Thomas Alva Edison

evidence.claim: At Samish Bay, Chuckanut Drive turns from farmland toward the mountain shore.
evidence.quote: The highway travels northwest through farmland at the north edge of the Skagit Valley

evidence.claim: Near Blanchard it crosses the railroad, then follows the west side of Blanchard Mountain at the southern end of the Chuckanut Mountains.
evidence.quote: The highway crosses over the railroad near Blanchard and turns northwest to follow Samish Bay around the west side of Blanchard Mountain at the south end of the Chuckanut Mountains.

evidence.claim: The railroad beside the farmland approach is the BNSF Bellingham Subdivision. Amtrak’s Cascades passenger trains use it too, sharing this coastal approach with the highway.
evidence.quote: generally following the BNSF Bellingham Subdivision, a railroad that also carries Amtrak's Cascades passenger trains.

evidence.claim: A local artist installed a Loch Ness Monster sculpture in the bay during the 2010s; it is visible from the road.
evidence.quote: A sculpture of the Loch Ness Monster in Samish Bay is visible from the road and was installed by a local artist in the 2010s.

evidence.claim: Farther along, the road passes an oyster farm before negotiating two hairpin turns at Oyster Creek.
evidence.quote: Chuckanut Drive then passes a Taylor Shellfish oyster farm and traverses a pair of hairpin turns at Oyster Creek near Pigeon Point.

evidence.claim: Washington’s first state park began with an offer of waterfront land along Chuckanut Drive.
evidence.quote: He mentioned this idea to Bellingham businessman Charles Larrabee, who agreed to deed waterfront property he owned in the area for the purpose.

evidence.claim: Washington’s first state park
evidence.quote: It was created in 1915 as Washington's first state park.

evidence.claim: Governor Ernest Lister proposed the park in 1913, and Charles Larrabee agreed to provide the property.
evidence.quote: In 1913, the governor of Washington, Ernest Lister, proposed establishing a park along Chuckanut Drive.

evidence.claim: Larrabee died the next year; his wife Frances completed the donation.
evidence.quote: He died in 1914, but his wife Frances made sure the deal went through to completion.

evidence.claim: Accepted by the state in 1915, it was first called Chuckanut State Park and renamed Larrabee in 1923.
evidence.quote: Initially called Chuckanut State Park, the park's name was changed to Larrabee in 1923.

evidence.claim: Accepted by the state in 1915
evidence.quote: On November 22, 1915, Washington State Board of Park Commissioners formally accepted it as well

evidence.claim: In 1936, Works Progress Administration funding helped add a water system, playground equipment and kitchen shelters. The following year, the Larrabee family donated another 1,500 acres.
evidence.quote:
In 1936, the Works Progress Administration provided US$30,000 in federal funding, leading to improvements such as playground equipment, a water system, and kitchen shelters.
The Larrabee family donated another 1500 acres in 1937

evidence.claim: Clayton Beach has sandstone formations and tidepools, with views across Samish Bay toward the San Juan Islands.
evidence.quote: The area provides views of Samish Bay and the San Juan Islands and contains sandstone formations and tidepools.
